biology-cell-quest.subject: Biology
biology-cell-quest.title: The Cell Quest: Explore the Building Blocks of Life
biology-cell-quest.hook: What tiny structure makes every living thing possible?
biology-cell-quest.concept: Cells are the basic structural and functional units of living organisms. Some organisms consist of one cell; plants and animals are made of many specialised cells.

steps.heading: Meet the cell
steps.body: A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out life processes. Think of it as a tiny living workshop.

steps.heading: Inside the cell
steps.body: The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. Cytoplasm is where many reactions happen. The nucleus contains genetic information in plant and animal cells.

steps.heading: Plant cell clue
steps.body: Plant cells usually have a cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large permanent vacuole.

biology-cell-quest.question: Which cell structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
biology-cell-quest.explanation: The cell membrane forms a selective boundary around the cell.
biology-cell-quest.voiceover: Welcome, explorer! Today we investigate cells, the tiny building blocks of life. Cells are the smallest units that carry out life processes. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves. The nucleus contains genetic information. Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole. Your challenge: which structure controls what enters and leaves? Pause and choose. The answer is the cell membrane. Great discovery!

chemistry-atoms-quest.subject: Chemistry
chemistry-atoms-quest.title: Atom Adventure: What Is Everything Made Of?
chemistry-atoms-quest.hook: Can you imagine building the world from tiny particles?
chemistry-atoms-quest.concept: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that retains that element's chemical properties. Atoms contain protons, neutrons and electrons.

steps.heading: The centre
steps.body: The nucleus is at the centre of an atom. It contains positively charged protons and neutral neutrons.

steps.heading: Around the nucleus
steps.body: Negatively charged electrons occupy regions around the nucleus called energy levels or shells in a simple model.

steps.heading: Element identity
steps.body: The number of protons is the atomic number. It identifies the element.

chemistry-atoms-quest.question: Which particle determines the atomic number?
chemistry-atoms-quest.explanation: The atomic number equals the number of protons in an atom's nucleus.
chemistry-atoms-quest.voiceover: Welcome to the Atom Adventure! Everything around us is made from atoms. At the centre is a nucleus containing positive protons and neutral neutrons. Negative electrons occupy regions around the nucleus. The number of protons tells us which element an atom is. Challenge time: which particle determines the atomic number? Pause and choose. It is the proton. Keep exploring!

physics-forces-quest.subject: Physics
physics-forces-quest.title: Force Mission: Push, Pull and Motion
physics-forces-quest.hook: What makes a football speed up, slow down or change direction?
physics-forces-quest.concept: A force is a push or pull. Forces can change an object's motion or shape. The SI unit of force is the newton (N).

steps.heading: Push or pull
steps.body: Kicking a ball is a push. Pulling a door open is a pull. Both are forces.

steps.heading: Balanced forces
steps.body: If forces are balanced, the resultant force is zero. An object's motion does not change.

steps.heading: Unbalanced forces
steps.body: An unbalanced resultant force changes motion: an object may speed up, slow down or turn.

physics-forces-quest.question: What is the resultant force when forces are balanced?
physics-forces-quest.explanation: Balanced forces cancel, so the resultant force is zero newtons.
physics-forces-quest.voiceover: Welcome to Force Mission! A force is a push or a pull. A kick pushes a football; opening a door can involve a pull. Forces can be balanced or unbalanced. Balanced forces cancel and give a resultant force of zero. Unbalanced forces change motion. Your challenge: what is the resultant force when forces are balanced? Pause and choose. The answer is zero newtons!

geography-water-cycle.subject: Geography
geography-water-cycle.title: Water Cycle Adventure: Follow a Drop
geography-water-cycle.hook: How can the same water travel from a river to a cloud and back?
geography-water-cycle.concept: The water cycle moves water between Earth's surface and atmosphere through processes including evaporation, condensation and precipitation.

steps.heading: Evaporation
steps.body: Energy from the Sun causes liquid water to change into water vapour.

steps.heading: Condensation
steps.body: As water vapour cools, it forms tiny droplets that make clouds.

steps.heading: Precipitation
steps.body: Water falls from clouds as rain, snow or hail, then collects or flows across the land.

geography-water-cycle.question: What is the change from water vapour into tiny liquid droplets called?
geography-water-cycle.explanation: Condensation happens when water vapour cools and changes into liquid droplets.
geography-water-cycle.voiceover: Follow one drop on a Water Cycle Adventure! The Sun provides energy for evaporation, changing liquid water into water vapour. Higher in the atmosphere, cooling vapour condenses into tiny droplets that form clouds. Then precipitation brings water back as rain, snow or hail. Water collects in rivers, lakes and oceans, and the cycle continues. Challenge: what is vapour cooling into droplets called? Condensation!

history-great-zimbabwe.subject: History
history-great-zimbabwe.title: Great Zimbabwe: The Stone City That Connected Africa to the World
history-great-zimbabwe.hook: A city of stone. A network of ocean trade. Who built Great Zimbabwe?
history-great-zimbabwe.concept: Great Zimbabwe was a major Shona city and trading centre in southern Africa. Built and expanded between about 1100 and 1450, it is famous for its carefully fitted granite walls made without mortar.

steps.heading: A city on the plateau
steps.body: Shona communities built and expanded Great Zimbabwe between about 1100 and 1450. It became a major political and trading centre in southern Africa.

steps.heading: Walls without cement
steps.body: Builders shaped naturally splitting granite into blocks and fitted them in carefully layered, curving walls without mortar.

steps.heading: Trade across the ocean
steps.body: Archaeologists found imported glass beads, porcelain and coins. These finds show Great Zimbabwe was linked to trade networks reaching the Indian Ocean.

history-great-zimbabwe.question: What is distinctive about Great Zimbabwe's famous stone walls?
options: They were joined with modern cement
They were built from fitted stone without mortar
They were made from fired bricks
history-great-zimbabwe.explanation: The builders fitted granite stones together in dry-stone walls without mortar.
history-great-zimbabwe.voiceover: A city of stone. A network of ocean trade. Who built Great Zimbabwe? Shona communities built and expanded this remarkable city between about eleven hundred and fourteen fifty. Its builders shaped granite into carefully fitted walls, without using mortar. And this was no isolated settlement. Archaeologists found imported glass beads, porcelain and coins, evidence of links reaching the Indian Ocean. Quick challenge: what made its walls special? They were built from fitted stone without mortar. This is Great Zimbabwe.

computing-algorithms.subject: Computer Science
computing-algorithms.title: Algorithm Adventure: Give the Computer a Plan
computing-algorithms.hook: How does a computer know what to do next?
computing-algorithms.concept: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task.

steps.heading: Step-by-step
steps.body: An algorithm breaks a task into clear steps that can be followed in order.

steps.heading: Sequence matters
steps.body: Changing the order of instructions can change the result. A recipe is a familiar example.

steps.heading: Test the plan
steps.body: Try the algorithm, check the result and improve any unclear or incorrect steps.

computing-algorithms.question: What is an algorithm?
options: A finite set of ordered instructions
computing-algorithms.explanation: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions to solve a problem.
computing-algorithms.voiceover: Welcome to Algorithm Adventure! An algorithm is a finite set of ordered instructions for solving a problem. Think about making a sandwich: the steps need to be clear and in a sensible order. If instructions are missing or mixed up, the result may be wrong. Test your plan and improve it. Challenge: what is an algorithm? It is a finite set of ordered instructions!

business-enterprise.subject: Business Studies
business-enterprise.title: Young Entrepreneur Quest: Spot an Opportunity
business-enterprise.hook: Can a simple problem become a useful business idea?
business-enterprise.concept: An entrepreneur identifies an opportunity, organises resources and takes calculated risks to provide a product or service.

steps.heading: Find a need
steps.body: Notice a problem people want solved. Ask who needs help and what would be useful.

steps.heading: Plan resources
steps.body: Consider materials, skills, time, costs and the people who may buy the product or service.

steps.heading: Test and improve
steps.body: Ask potential customers for feedback and improve the idea before expanding.

business-enterprise.question: What does an entrepreneur do?
business-enterprise.explanation: Entrepreneurs identify opportunities and organise resources to create value.
business-enterprise.voiceover: Welcome to Young Entrepreneur Quest! Entrepreneurs look for opportunities to solve problems. They plan the resources they need, such as materials, skills, time and money. They also listen to customers and improve their ideas. Challenge: what does an entrepreneur do? An entrepreneur identifies opportunities and organises resources to create value. What problem could you solve in your community?

shona-proverbs.subject: Shona
shona-proverbs.title: Shona Language Quest: Meaning Beyond Words
shona-proverbs.hook: Can a short proverb teach a big lesson?
shona-proverbs.concept: Proverbs are traditional expressions that communicate shared wisdom, values and experience. Meaning depends on context and cultural understanding.

steps.heading: Listen carefully
steps.body: Notice the words, imagery and situation in which a proverb is used.

steps.heading: Find the lesson
steps.body: Ask what advice or observation the proverb communicates. Avoid translating word-for-word only.

steps.heading: Use context
steps.body: Discuss who might use the proverb, when it is appropriate and what values it reflects.

shona-proverbs.question: What helps us understand the meaning of a proverb?
shona-proverbs.explanation: Context and cultural knowledge help explain a proverb's intended lesson.
shona-proverbs.voiceover: Welcome to Shona Language Quest! Proverbs carry wisdom through memorable expressions. To understand one, listen to the words and consider the situation where it is used. Ask what lesson it teaches and what values it reflects. A direct word-for-word translation may miss the deeper meaning. Challenge: what helps us understand a proverb? Context and cultural understanding!

art-colour-theory.subject: Art & Design
art-colour-theory.title: Colour Quest: Build a Strong Palette
art-colour-theory.hook: Why do some colours feel calm while others grab attention?
art-colour-theory.concept: Colour theory describes relationships between colours. Primary colours are starting points for mixing; complementary colours sit opposite each other on a colour wheel.

steps.heading: Primary colours
steps.body: In the traditional artists' paint model, red, yellow and blue are commonly taught as primary colours.

steps.heading: Mixing colours
steps.body: Mixing primary pigments can create secondary colours such as orange, green and violet.

steps.heading: Contrast
steps.body: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on a colour wheel and can create strong visual contrast.

art-colour-theory.question: Where are complementary colours found on a colour wheel?
art-colour-theory.explanation: Complementary colours are opposite one another on the colour wheel.
art-colour-theory.voiceover: Welcome to Colour Quest! Artists use colour relationships to create mood and contrast. In the traditional paint model, red, yellow and blue are primary colours. Mixing them can make orange, green and violet. Complementary colours sit opposite each other on a colour wheel and create strong contrast. Challenge: where do you find complementary colours? Opposite each other!

maths-fractions.subject: Mathematics
maths-fractions.title: Fraction Adventure: Parts of a Whole
maths-fractions.hook: If you share a pizza equally, how can you describe each piece?
maths-fractions.concept: A fraction represents part of a whole or a ratio. The denominator tells how many equal parts make the whole; the numerator tells how many parts are selected.

steps.heading: Denominator
steps.body: The bottom number tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into.

steps.heading: Numerator
steps.body: The top number tells how many of those parts are being counted.

steps.heading: Equivalent fractions
steps.body: Fractions can look different but have the same value, such as one half and two quarters.

maths-fractions.question: In the fraction 3/4, what does the 4 represent?
maths-fractions.explanation: The denominator 4 means the whole is divided into four equal parts.
maths-fractions.voiceover: Welcome to Fraction Adventure! A fraction describes part of a whole. The bottom number is the denominator: it tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number is the numerator: it tells how many parts we count. Three quarters means three out of four equal parts. Challenge: in three quarters, what does four represent? The four equal parts in the whole!

science-states-matter.subject: General Science
science-states-matter.title: Matter Mission: Solid, Liquid or Gas?
science-states-matter.hook: Why can ice melt, water flow and steam spread out?
science-states-matter.concept: Matter commonly exists as solids, liquids and gases. Heating or cooling can change a substance's state.

steps.heading: Solid
steps.body: A solid has a fixed shape and volume. Its particles are close together and vibrate around fixed positions.

steps.heading: Liquid
steps.body: A liquid has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Its particles can move past one another.

steps.heading: Gas
steps.body: A gas has no fixed shape or volume and spreads to fill its container.

science-states-matter.question: Which state has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container?
science-states-matter.explanation: A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
science-states-matter.voiceover: Welcome to Matter Mission! Matter commonly exists as solids, liquids and gases. A solid keeps its shape and volume. A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container. A gas spreads out to fill its container. Heating and cooling can change a substance's state. Challenge: which state has a fixed volume but takes the container's shape? Liquid!

library-source-check.subject: Library Skills
library-source-check.title: Information Detective: Check Your Sources
library-source-check.hook: How can you tell whether an online claim is trustworthy?
library-source-check.concept: Evaluating information means checking its author, evidence, date, purpose and agreement with other reliable sources.

steps.heading: Who made it?
steps.body: Look for the author or organisation and ask whether they have relevant expertise.

steps.heading: Where is the evidence?
steps.body: Check whether claims are supported by trustworthy evidence and links to original sources.

steps.heading: When and why?
steps.body: Check the publication date and consider whether the purpose is to inform, persuade or sell.

library-source-check.question: Which is a useful first step when checking an online claim?
options: Check who published it and the evidence
Trust it because it looks professional
library-source-check.explanation: Checking the source and its supporting evidence is a strong first step.
library-source-check.voiceover: Welcome, Information Detective! Not every online claim is reliable. Start by checking who published it and whether they have relevant expertise. Look for evidence and original sources. Check the date because information can become outdated. Ask whether the purpose is to inform, persuade or sell. Challenge: what is a useful first step? Check who published the claim and the evidence!

apollo-13-rescue.subject: History and Space Science
apollo-13-rescue.title: Apollo 13: The Mission That Found a Way Home
apollo-13-rescue.hook: Apollo 13 was meant to land on the Moon. Then an oxygen tank ruptured—and the mission became a race to bring three astronauts home.
apollo-13-rescue.concept: Apollo 13 launched on 11 April 1970. After an oxygen-system failure in the Service Module on 13 April, the Moon landing was cancelled. The crew used the Lunar Module Aquarius for life support during the return journey and splashed down safely on 17 April.

steps.heading: A mission to the Moon
steps.body: James Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise launched aboard Apollo 13 on 11 April 1970, aiming to land in the Fra Mauro region.

steps.heading: A serious systems failure
steps.body: On 13 April, an oxygen tank in the Service Module ruptured. The Command and Service Module could no longer provide its normal power, oxygen and water supplies.

steps.heading: A team finds a way home
steps.body: The crew used the Lunar Module Aquarius as a lifeboat. Flight controllers and engineers on the ground helped plan the return, and the crew splashed down safely on 17 April.

apollo-13-rescue.question: What role did the Lunar Module Aquarius play after the oxygen-system failure?
options: It became a temporary lifeboat for the crew
It landed the crew on the Moon
It replaced the Saturn V rocket
apollo-13-rescue.explanation: Aquarius provided life support, power, propulsion and guidance during the return to Earth.
apollo-13-rescue.voiceover: Apollo 13 was meant to land on the Moon. Then an oxygen tank ruptured—and the mission became a race to bring three astronauts home. On 11 April 1970, astronauts Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise launched toward the Moon. Two days later, an oxygen tank in the Service Module ruptured. The planned landing was called off. The crew moved into the Lunar Module, Aquarius, and used it as a lifeboat. Back on Earth, flight controllers and engineers worked with the astronauts to plan their return. On 17 April, all three astronauts splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean. Apollo 13 became a powerful example of teamwork and problem-solving. Now, one question: what role did Aquarius play? It served as a temporary lifeboat.

sources.title: Apollo 13 Post-Launch Mission Operations Report (28 April 1970)

history-antikythera-mechanism.subject: History and Technology
history-antikythera-mechanism.title: The Antikythera Mechanism: A 2,000-Year-Old Computer
history-antikythera-mechanism.hook: A shipwreck hides a 2,000-year-old machine. Could it predict the sky?
history-antikythera-mechanism.concept: The Antikythera Mechanism was an ancient Greek geared device, built around 150–100 BCE. It used interlocking bronze gears and dials to calculate astronomical cycles, including the movements of the Sun and Moon and the timing of eclipses.

steps.heading: A discovery beneath the sea
steps.body: In 1901, sponge divers recovered strange bronze fragments from an ancient shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera.

steps.heading: A machine of tiny gears
steps.body: Researchers identified about 30 toothed gears, dials and Greek inscriptions. The surviving device is preserved in 82 fragments.

steps.heading: Predicting the sky
steps.body: Turning its mechanism moved pointers that displayed astronomical cycles, including the Sun, Moon and eclipse predictions.

history-antikythera-mechanism.question: What made the Antikythera Mechanism so remarkable?
options: It used gears to calculate astronomical cycles
It sent messages across the sea
history-antikythera-mechanism.explanation: Its interlocking gears converted cycles into useful calendar and astronomical predictions.
history-antikythera-mechanism.voiceover: A shipwreck hides a two-thousand-year-old machine. Could it predict the sky? In 1901, sponge divers found strange bronze fragments in an ancient shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera. Scientists discovered a complex device with about thirty toothed gears, dials and Greek inscriptions. Its moving pointers displayed astronomical cycles, including the movements of the Sun and Moon, and helped predict eclipses. It was built more than two thousand years ago, yet it worked like a mechanical calculator. Quick challenge: what made it remarkable? Interlocking gears that calculated the sky. Ancient engineering was astonishing!
